faq.q: Why do electric guitars need steel strings?
faq.a: The pickup only senses magnetic metal. Steel strings become slightly magnetised by the pickup's magnet, so their vibrations disturb its field. Nylon strings would make no signal.
asks: Do nylon strings work on an electric guitar?

faq.q: What does the magnet in a pickup do?
faq.a: It magnetises the part of the string just above it. When that magnetised string vibrates, the magnetic field through the coil wobbles in the same rhythm.
asks: Why is there a magnet under the strings?

faq.q: How does the pickup coil make a signal?
faq.a: The coil is thousands of turns of very fine wire around the magnets. As the vibrating string changes the magnetic field, a tiny alternating voltage is induced in the coil.
asks: How many turns are in a pickup?

faq.q: Why does an electric guitar need an amplifier?
faq.a: A solid electric guitar is quiet on its own and the pickup's signal is tiny. An amplifier boosts it to drive a speaker, and can also shape the sound, for example adding distortion.
asks: Why is an electric guitar quiet unplugged?

faq.q: Why do some guitars have more than one pickup?
faq.a: A pickup near the neck senses the wide middle of the string's swing and sounds warm; one near the bridge senses a stiffer part and sounds brighter. Switching between them changes the tone.
asks: What does the pickup switch do?

facts: Typical guitar pickups have several thousand turns of very fine copper wire.
Magnetic pickups need steel or nickel strings; nylon strings produce no signal.
